title: Marsh accretion and the sediment budget
bodyMd:
A salt marsh keeps pace with a rising sea by gaining elevation in two ways: it traps mineral sediment carried in on the tide, and it accumulates the roots and stems its own plants leave behind. The two contributions are linked. A marsh that has fallen low relative to the tide floods more deeply and for longer, which delivers more suspended sediment to its surface and, within limits, encourages the growth of the grasses whose litter becomes the organic fraction. Coastal engineers have long admired an arrangement in which falling behind is itself the mechanism of catching up.

Vogel argues that this self-correction has been overstated, because it presumes a supply of mineral sediment that many estuaries no longer have. Dams hold back material that once travelled down the rivers to the coast; across the estuaries she surveyed, the suspended load measured at the head of tide has fallen by more than half since 1950. Where the flooding water carries little sediment, a low marsh receives more water but not more material, and only the organic half of the feedback remains — a half that is itself curtailed once flooding grows deep enough to stress the grasses.

Vogel's critics point to a source her method could not register. Measuring at the head of tide records what the rivers deliver, not what the estuary erodes from its own bed and banks and carries landward onto the marshes; in some systems that internal supply exceeds the riverine one. Vogel accepts the omission but not its force: the internal supply, she replies, draws down a finite stock rather than being renewed, and so can postpone a sediment deficit without preventing one.

Where the flooding water carries little sediment, a low marsh receives more water but not more material, so only the organic half of the feedback remains, and that half is itself curtailed once flooding grows deep enough to stress the grasses. provenance.notes: Original passage written for the wave 4 top-up to support a new Reading Comprehension set and to carry a clean replacement for the quarantined multi-select item gre-verbal-rc-commonplace-registers-221. Salt-marsh accretion, sediment starvation below dams and the organic-versus-mineral distinction are real subjects in coastal geomorphology, but the researcher Vogel, the survey, the more-than-half figure, the critics' objection and every sentence of the wording are invented for this item set. Nothing here is taken from, or paraphrased from, any ETS passage or any real publication. Every fact needed by the three questions built on it is stated in the passage itself.
